bibliography.note: Chow-Fraser, P. & Sprules, W. G. 1992. Type-3 functional response in limnetic suspension-feeders, as demonstrated by in situ grazing rates. Hydrobiologia 232(3): 175–191, doi:10.1007/BF00013703 — as cited

claims.claim: 1-mm cladocerans: field maximum clearance 15.35 mL/animal/d; maximum ingestion 40.65 µg fresh wt/d; incipient limiting level ≈ 2,650 µg fresh wt/L
claims.quote: We divided this value by the maximum filtering rate (MFR) of 15.35 ml/animal/d
claims.conditions: composite of published in-situ (Haney-chamber) grazing rates interpolated to a 1-mm animal from filtering-rate–length regressions (Chow-Fraser & Knoechel 1985; Knoechel & Holtby 1986; Haney 1985); mostly daphniids (Daphnia galeata, D. dubia, D. rosea; also Diaphanosoma, Holopedium, Ceriodaphnia); 'edible' algae < 30–31 µm; fresh weight from a f.w.:d.w. ratio of 3.44; MIR from a Lineweaver–Burk (type-2) fit; ILC = MIR/MFR = 2.65 × 10³ µg/L
claims.note: The authors say the MIR/MFR/ILC exercise was 'solely for the purpose of comparing laboratory and field data, and was not intended to provide definitive parameters' (p. 183). The paper's '≈ 0.35 mg C/L†' is a project conversion: 2,650 ÷ 3.44 = 770 µg DW/L, × ~0.45 C = ~0.35 mg C/L; the 3.44 ratio is the source's, the carbon fraction is not.

claims.claim: diaptomid adults: field maximum clearance 4.9 mL/animal/d; maximum ingestion 0.94 µg fresh wt/d; incipient limiting level ≈ 190 µg fresh wt/L
claims.quote: We divided this value by MFR of 4.9 ml/animal/d to obtain an ILC
claims.conditions: adult Diaptomus minutus (0.70–0.85 mm prosome) and D. oregonensis (0.9–1.4 mm), not standardized to 1 mm; tracer algae 4–8 µm and an 'edible' limit of < 10 µm, so the response 'will only apply to their feeding on small algal particles (< 10 µm)' (p. 181); the MIR fit includes Richman's (1964) bottle-and-isotope data, which the authors say are 'not directly comparable to the in situ data'; ILC 0.19 × 10³ µg/L
claims.note: '≈ 25 µg C/L†' is the same project conversion (190 ÷ 3.44 × ~0.45)

claims.source_value: lakes and ponds of Ontario and Michigan; experiments at 16–23 °C (cladoceran studies 16–22 and 22 °C; diaptomid studies 17–23 °C); the diaptomid high-food points (Richman 1964, 22–23 °C) came from bottles with isotope-labelled natural nanoplankton, not chambers
claims.location: p. 179 (PDF p. 5), Description of field studies and Table 1; p. 180 (PDF p. 6), Table 2
claims.quote: The study sites in this paper include lakes and ponds of Ontario and Michigan
claims.conditions: daytime (10:00–17:00) incubations of 5–20 min with labelled tracer algae or yeast
claims.note: suggested: 'compiled in-situ grazing studies, Ontario and Michigan lakes, 16–23 °C; diaptomids on < 10-µm algae'

claims.claim: Calanoids saturate at about one-fourteenth of the cladocerans' food level with a type-3 response in the field (Chow-Fraser & Sprules 1992)
claims.quote: The overall shape of this curve is therefore most consistent with a Type 3
claims.conditions: diaptomid filtering rates rose with algal concentration up to about 2 × 10² µg/L (n = 8, r = 0.99) and then declined; for cladocerans, rates below 10³ µg/L rose with log food (n = 10) and above it fell (n = 5)
claims.note: ILC 2.65 × 10³ ÷ 0.19 × 10³ = 13.9, i.e. about one-fourteenth. 'Calanoids' rests on two Diaptomus species feeding on small algae (< 10 µm). The '0.4 times (0.3–1 times)' per-biomass clearance is a project estimate; its body-mass inputs are not in this paper.

notes: Laboratory comparisons in the same paper: Daphnia ILCs 1–8.5 × 10³ µg/L (more than half 1–3 × 10³); laboratory copepod ILCs 0.5–2.8 × 10³ µg/L, higher than the field D. minutus value; Daphnia filtering after 2 h acclimation to low food rose 4–5-fold over unacclimated animals and fell again after > 70 h (emaciation). The authors explain the field type-3 response in cladocerans by low body carbon at chronically low food, but say this cannot explain it in diaptomids.
